# Mahāpiṅgalajātaka (Ja 240)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāpiṅgalajātaka* (Ja 240) is a story found in the *Jātaka* collection of the Pali Canon, located as the tenth and concluding discourse of the *Upāhanavagga* in the second *nipāta* [Fausböll 1879]. According to the traditional introductory setting (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha recounted the story while staying at the Jetavana monastery near Sāvatthī, prompted by the actions and fate of Devadatta [Fausböll 1879].

The narrative relates the death of the tyrannical king Mahāpiṅgala of Benares [Winternitz 1933; Fausböll 1897]. While all the citizens of Benares rejoice at the death of their oppressive ruler, a doorkeeper (*dovārika*) is found weeping [Winternitz 1933]. When questioned by the Bodhisatta, the king's righteous son and successor, the doorkeeper explains that he weeps not out of affection, but out of fear: the king routinely delivered eight blows to his head whenever ascending or descending the palace stairs, and he dreads what suffering the tyrant might inflict upon the rulers of the netherworld or whether he might somehow return [Winternitz 1933; Fausböll 1879]. In the formal identification of characters (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the tyrannical King Piṅgala as Devadatta and the Bodhisatta as his son [Fausböll 1879; Fausböll 1897].
